sections.title: Present Tense Regular Verbs
sections.rule: Drop the -ar/-er/-ir ending and add person endings. -ar: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -ais, -am. -er: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -eis, -em. -ir: -o, -es, -e, -imos, -is, -em. Unlike Spanish, the nós ending keeps the theme vowel long only in writing.
sections.example_target: Eu falo português e ela come frutas todos os dias.
sections.example_target_2: Nós partimos amanhã de manhã.
sections.example_ref: English: I speak Portuguese and she eats fruit every day. / We leave tomorrow morning.
sections.note: Brazilians rarely use vós; the tu form is often replaced by você, which takes the third-person (ele/ela) ending: você fala, você come.

sections.title: Ser vs Estar vs Ficar
sections.rule: Ser marks identity and permanent traits (Sou brasileiro). Estar marks temporary states and location of people/things (Estou cansado). Ficar means to become, to stay, or the fixed location of places (A escola fica aqui).
sections.example_target: Ela é médica, mas hoje está doente.
sections.example_target_2: O banco fica perto da praça e eu fico nervoso lá.
sections.example_ref: English: She is a doctor, but today she is sick. / The bank is near the square and I get nervous there.
sections.note: Use ficar, not ser/estar, for where a permanent place is located: O Rio fica no Brasil (not é/está).

sections.title: Pretérito Perfeito (Simple Past)
sections.rule: The main past tense for finished actions. Regular -ar: -ei, -aste, -ou, -amos, -astes, -aram; -er: -i, -este, -eu, -emos, -estes, -eram; -ir: -i, -iste, -iu, -imos, -istes, -iram. Key irregulars: ser/ir share fui/foi/foram; ter = tive/teve; fazer = fiz/fez; poder = pude/pôde.
sections.example_target: Ontem eu falei com o João e fiz o jantar.
sections.example_target_2: Eles foram ao cinema e voltaram tarde.
sections.example_ref: English: Yesterday I spoke with João and made dinner. / They went to the movies and came back late.
sections.note: Ser and ir are identical in this tense: fui can mean 'I was' or 'I went' — context decides.

sections.title: The Personal Infinitive
sections.rule: Portuguese has an infinitive that inflects for person: falar, falares, falar, falarmos, falardes, falarem. Use it when the infinitive has its own subject, especially after prepositions, to make clear who does the action.
sections.example_target: É importante vocês chegarem cedo.
sections.example_target_2: Ao saírmos de casa, começou a chover.
sections.example_ref: English: It's important that you (all) arrive early. / As we left the house, it started to rain.
sections.note: This form is unique to Portuguese. For the nós and eles subjects it adds -mos and -em to the whole infinitive: falarmos, falarem.

sections.title: Mandatory Contractions
sections.rule: Prepositions merge with articles and must be contracted in writing. em+o=no, em+a=na, de+o=do, de+a=da, a+o=ao, a+a=à, por+o=pelo, por+a=pela, em+um=num, de+este=deste.
sections.example_target: Vou ao mercado e depois passo na farmácia.
sections.example_target_2: O livro do professor está na mesa.
sections.example_ref: English: I'm going to the market and then I'll stop by the pharmacy. / The teacher's book is on the table.
sections.note: a + a = à carries a grave accent (crase): Vou à praia. This à is pronounced the same as plain a.

sections.title: Near Future with Ir
sections.rule: The everyday future is ir (present) + infinitive: vou, vais/vai, vamos, ides, vão + verb. It expresses plans and imminent actions and is far more common in speech than the simple future.
sections.example_target: Eu vou viajar no próximo mês.
sections.example_target_2: Nós vamos comer pizza hoje à noite.
sections.example_ref: English: I'm going to travel next month. / We're going to eat pizza tonight.
sections.note: Unlike English, do not add a preposition: say vou comer, never vou a comer (that construction is European and less common in Brazil).

sections.title: Object Pronouns & Placement
sections.rule: Direct objects: me, te, o/a, nos, vos, os/as. Indirect: me, te, lhe, nos, vos, lhes. In Brazilian Portuguese the pronoun usually comes before the verb (proclisis): Ele me viu. After the verb (enclisis, with a hyphen) is standard in Portugal and formal writing.
sections.example_target: Eu te amo e nunca vou te esquecer.
sections.example_target_2: A gente lhe deu o presente ontem.
sections.example_ref: English: I love you and I'll never forget you. / We gave him/her the gift yesterday.
sections.note: Spoken Brazilian often replaces o/a with ele/ela after a verb: Eu vi ele (I saw him), instead of the formal Eu o vi.

sections.title: Diminutives with -inho
sections.rule: Add -inho/-inha (or -zinho/-zinha after stressed vowels or certain endings) to soften, show affection, or shrink. It agrees in gender and number: cafezinho, casinha, cachorrinhos. It often signals warmth rather than small size.
sections.example_target: Vamos tomar um cafezinho e comer um pãozinho.
sections.example_target_2: Que bebê fofinho, olha as mãozinhas dele!
sections.example_ref: English: Let's have a little coffee and eat a little bread roll. / What a cute little baby, look at his little hands!
sections.note: Diminutives are hugely common in Brazil and often mean 'nice/quick,' not literally small: um minutinho = 'just a moment,' obrigadinho = a warm 'thanks.'

sections.title: Pretérito Imperfeito
sections.rule: Describes habitual, ongoing, or background past actions ('used to,' 'was doing'). -ar: -ava endings (falava); -er/-ir: -ia endings (comia, partia). Only four verbs are irregular: ser (era), ter (tinha), vir (vinha), pôr (punha), plus ir (ia).
sections.example_target: Quando eu era criança, brincava na rua todos os dias.
sections.example_target_2: Ela sempre tinha um livro na bolsa.
sections.example_ref: English: When I was a child, I used to play in the street every day. / She always had a book in her bag.
sections.note: Use the imperfeito for the setting and repeated actions, and the perfeito for the single completed event that interrupts them: Eu dormia quando o telefone tocou.

sections.title: Present Subjunctive
sections.rule: The presente do subjuntivo expresses wishes, doubt, and emotion after que. Take the eu present form, drop -o, then -ar verbs take -e endings (fale) and -er/-ir verbs take -a endings (coma). Triggered by espero que, é importante que, talvez, and future quando.
sections.example_target: Espero que você fale com ele hoje.
sections.example_target_2: Talvez nós sejamos os primeiros a chegar.
sections.example_ref: English: I hope you talk to him today. / Maybe we'll be the first to arrive.
sections.note: Irregular stems come from the eu form: ter → tenha, fazer → faça, ser → seja, ir → vá, saber → saiba, dar → dê.

sections.title: Conditional (Futuro do Pretérito)
sections.rule: Formed on the full infinitive + -ia, -ias, -ia, -íamos, -íeis, -iam: falaria, comeria, partiria. It expresses hypotheticals and polite requests. Three verbs shorten the stem: dizer → diria, fazer → faria, trazer → traria.
sections.example_target: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
sections.example_target_2: Com mais tempo, nós viajaríamos pelo mundo.
sections.example_ref: English: I would like a coffee, please. / With more time, we would travel the world.
sections.note: In casual speech Brazilians often replace the conditional with the imperfeito: Eu queria um café sounds more natural than Eu gostaria in everyday talk.

sections.title: The Imperative
sections.rule: Affirmative tu uses the bare present stem (fala, come, abre). Affirmative and all negative commands for você/vocês borrow the subjunctive (fale, coma; não fale, não fales). Brazilians mostly use the você forms even when saying 'you.'
sections.example_target: Fale mais devagar, por favor!
sections.example_target_2: Não coma tão rápido e beba água.
sections.example_ref: English: Speak more slowly, please! / Don't eat so fast and drink water.
sections.note: In spoken Brazil the tu-style affirmative (fala, vem, olha) is extremely common even with você: Vem cá! Olha isso!

sections.title: Comparatives & Superlatives
sections.rule: Comparisons use mais/menos + adjective + (do) que: mais alto do que. Equality uses tão + adjective + quanto. Superlative: o/a mais + adjective + de. Irregulars: bom→melhor, mau→pior, grande→maior, pequeno→menor.
sections.example_target: Ela é mais alta do que eu, mas ele é o mais alto de todos.
sections.example_target_2: Este restaurante é melhor do que aquele.
sections.example_ref: English: She is taller than I am, but he is the tallest of all. / This restaurant is better than that one.
sections.note: The absolute superlative -íssimo means 'extremely': bonito → bonitíssimo, fácil → facílimo, difícil → dificílimo.

sections.title: Reflexive & Pronominal Verbs
sections.rule: Reflexive pronouns me, te, se, nos, vos, se pair with verbs like levantar-se, chamar-se, sentir-se, lembrar-se de. In Brazil the pronoun normally precedes the verb: Eu me levanto cedo. Many take fixed prepositions (lembrar-se de, esquecer-se de).
sections.example_target: Eu me chamo Ana e me sinto bem hoje.
sections.example_target_2: Nós nos lembramos daquele dia.
sections.example_ref: English: My name is Ana and I feel good today. / We remember that day.
sections.note: Brazilians frequently drop the reflexive pronoun in casual speech: Eu levanto às sete instead of Eu me levanto às sete.

sections.title: Present Continuous
sections.rule: For actions happening right now, Brazil uses estar + gerúndio (verb + -ndo): estou falando, está comendo, estamos partindo. (Portugal uses estar a + infinitive: estou a falar.) Form the gerúndio by replacing -r with -ndo.
sections.example_target: Estou estudando português agora.
sections.example_target_2: Eles estão comendo no jardim.
sections.example_ref: English: I'm studying Portuguese right now. / They are eating in the garden.
sections.note: The gerúndio is invariable — it never changes for gender or number: ela está falando, eles estão falando.

sections.title: Relative Pronouns
sections.rule: Que (that/which/who) is the all-purpose relative for people and things. Quem refers to people after a preposition. O qual/a qual adds clarity or follows prepositions. Cujo/cuja means 'whose' and agrees with the thing owned. Onde means 'where.'
sections.example_target: O homem que vi era a pessoa com quem falei ontem.
sections.example_target_2: A escritora cujos livros adoro mora aqui.
sections.example_ref: English: The man I saw was the person I spoke with yesterday. / The writer whose books I love lives here.
sections.note: Cujo agrees with the possessed noun, not the owner: a mulher cujo carro (the woman whose car) — masculine because carro is masculine.

sections.title: Passive Voice
sections.rule: Analytic passive: ser + past participle, which agrees in gender and number (A casa foi construída; Os livros foram vendidos). The passive se (or apassivadora) works with transitive verbs: Vende-se casa; Alugam-se quartos; Fala-se inglês.
sections.example_target: O quadro foi pintado por uma artista famosa.
sections.example_target_2: Aqui se falam três línguas.
sections.example_ref: English: The painting was painted by a famous artist. / Three languages are spoken here.
sections.note: With passive se, the verb agrees with the noun: aluga-se um quarto (singular) but alugam-se quartos (plural).

sections.title: Pluperfect (Mais-que-perfeito Composto)
sections.rule: Formed with the imperfeito of ter + past participle: tinha falado, tinha comido. It marks an action completed before another past moment. The participle is invariable here (does not agree).
sections.example_target: Quando cheguei, ele já tinha saído.
sections.example_target_2: Nós tínhamos comido antes de você ligar.
sections.example_ref: English: When I arrived, he had already left. / We had eaten before you called.
sections.note: A one-word literary form exists (falara, comera) but is rare in speech — the tinha + participle version is the everyday choice.

sections.title: Perfect with Tenho + Participle
sections.rule: The pretérito perfeito composto uses the present of ter + participle: tenho falado, tenho estudado. Crucially, it expresses a repeated or continuous action from the past up to now — NOT a single finished event (unlike the Spanish/English present perfect).
sections.example_target: Tenho estudado muito nas últimas semanas.
sections.example_target_2: Ultimamente ele tem trabalhado demais.
sections.example_ref: English: I have been studying a lot in recent weeks. / Lately he has been working too much.
sections.note: For a single completed action, use the simple perfeito: 'I have already eaten' = Já comi, never Tenho comido (which would mean 'I've been eating repeatedly').

sections.title: Future Subjunctive
sections.rule: Unique to Portuguese, the futuro do subjuntivo appears after quando, se, enquanto, assim que when referring to real future conditions. For regular verbs it matches the infinitive: quando eu falar, se você quiser, se tivermos tempo. Irregulars use the perfeito stem (fui → for, fiz → fizer).
sections.example_target: Quando eu for ao Brasil, vou visitar Salvador.
sections.example_target_2: Se você quiser, a gente sai mais cedo.
sections.example_ref: English: When I go to Brazil, I'll visit Salvador. / If you want, we'll leave earlier.
sections.note: English uses the present here ('when I go'), but Portuguese requires this future subjunctive — a very common learner error is using the present indicative instead.

sections.title: Imperfect Subjunctive
sections.rule: The pretérito imperfeito do subjuntivo ends in -sse: falasse, comesse, fosse, tivesse. Build it from the eles perfeito form minus -ram, plus -sse endings (falaram → falasse). It follows past-tense triggers (queria que…) and hypothetical se clauses.
sections.example_target: Se eu fosse rico, viajaria o mundo inteiro.
sections.example_target_2: Ela queria que nós viéssemos mais cedo.
sections.example_ref: English: If I were rich, I would travel the whole world. / She wanted us to come earlier.
sections.note: The pattern for unreal conditions is: se + imperfect subjunctive, then conditional: Se eu tivesse tempo, ajudaria você.

sections.title: Third Conditional (Past Unreal)
sections.rule: For things that did not happen, use the conditional perfect teria + participle in the main clause and the pluperfect subjunctive tivesse + participle in the se clause. It expresses regret or hypothetical past outcomes.
sections.example_target: Se eu tivesse sabido, teria vindo mais cedo.
sections.example_target_2: Eles teriam ganhado se tivessem treinado mais.
sections.example_ref: English: If I had known, I would have come earlier. / They would have won if they had trained more.
sections.note: In casual Brazilian speech both halves are often replaced by the imperfeito: Se eu soubesse, eu vinha — grammatically loose but very common.
